package_info.package_manager: Custom/Unknown (malware distributed via document exploits, droppers, and removable media)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple variants (see SHA1 hashes in IOCs)
package_info.why_malicious: Mongall is a backdoor malware family used by the Aoqin Dragon APT group for cyberespionage. It is delivered via malicious documents exploiting MS Office vulnerabilities, fake removable devices, and phishing lures. The malware provides persistent remote access, command execution, and data exfiltration capabilities, and communicates with attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure.

execution_context.file_location: malicious Word document (exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Shellcode embedded in a malicious Word document exploiting CVE-2012-0158 to execute arbitrary code and drop Mongall payload.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the document is opened, the exploit triggers remote code execution, which writes and executes the Mongall backdoor binary on the victim system, establishing persistence and C2 communication.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of document exploits to execute arbitrary code is a hallmark of targeted malware campaigns.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Word documents should not contain or execute shellcode or drop executables.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; exploit code in documents is always malicious.
key_indicators: Presence of exploit code for CVE-2012-0158/CVE-2010-3333

execution_context.trigger: user double-clicks fake anti-virus link or opens malicious folder
execution_context.file_location: removable device or phishing lure (shortcut/link or executable)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Dropper executable that writes Mongall payload to disk and executes it, often using DLL hijacking or Themida packing for evasion.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At execution-time, the dropper writes the Mongall backdoor to disk, may use DLL hijacking to gain execution, and launches the backdoor process, enabling persistent access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Droppers that write and execute backdoor binaries are a classic malware delivery technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not silently install backdoors or use DLL hijacking.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may drop and execute new binaries, but not from phishing lures or removable devices.
key_indicators: Writes executable to disk from removable media or phishing link
Uses DLL hijacking or Themida packing

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Backdoor main loop: Connects to hardcoded C2 domains/IPs, receives commands, executes them (file operations, process manipulation, data exfiltration), and sends results back to C2.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the backdoor establishes a connection to attacker-controlled C2 servers, awaits instructions, executes arbitrary commands (including file exfiltration), and transmits results to the C2.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistent C2 communication and remote command execution are core backdoor behaviors.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not connect to suspicious C2 infrastructure or execute arbitrary remote commands.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools (RATs) may have similar features, but are not delivered via exploits or phishing.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: DNS tunneling module: Encodes C2 traffic in DNS queries/responses to evade detection.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the backdoor uses DNS tunneling to communicate with C2 servers, encoding commands and exfiltrated data in DNS traffic to bypass network monitoring.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DNS tunneling is a known technique for covert C2 communication and data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications do not encode command-and-control traffic in DNS queries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise tools use DNS for legitimate tunneling, but not in this context.

attack_chain.action: Initial access via phishing document exploiting MS Office vulnerabilities or via fake removable device/dropper.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of Mongall backdoor on victim system

attack_chain.action: Mongall backdoor is installed and persists on the system.
Backdoor establishes C2 connection, awaits commands, and exfiltrates data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing espionage, data theft, and remote control

behavioral_signatures: Execution of shellcode or PE files from Office documents
DLL hijacking or Themida-packed binaries launched from removable media or phishing lures
Persistent outbound connections to suspicious C2 domains/IPs
DNS tunneling activity with encoded payloads
file_indicators: Office documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333
Dropper executables with SHA1 hashes listed in IOCs
Mongall backdoor binaries (multiple SHA1s in IOCs)
network_indicators: Connections to C2 domains: back.satunusa.org, baomoi.vnptnet.info, bbw.fushing.org, etc.
Unusual DNS queries to attacker-controlled domains (DNS tunneling)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for Office documents exploiting known RCE vulnerabilities, execution of unknown binaries dropped from documents or removable media, and suspicious network activity including connections to known C2 domains/IPs and DNS tunneling patterns. Correlate file hashes with IOCs and watch for persistence mechanisms associated with Mongall and related backdoors.
